description: The OS layer the agents actually run on. Processes, threads, kernel/user split, system calls, context switches. Synchronisation primitives (mutex, spinlock, RW lock, semaphore, condition variable, futex). Scheduling (CFS, real-time, work stealing, affinity, NUMA awareness). IPC (pipes, sockets, shared memory, signals). Virtual memory at the OS level (VMA, page cache, swap, OOM). VFS + inode + dentry + file descriptor. Containers (namespaces + cgroups). Hypervisors + microVMs. The mechanisms that determine how parallel agent execution actually behaves on real hardware.
category_inheritance: genlMt → compiler_theory. OS correctness arguments map to compiler_theory's equivalence vocabulary: scheduling preserves program semantics (denotational); locks preserve invariants (referential transparency); fork's COW preserves observable behaviour (extensional); IPC ordering preserves causality (algebraic).

concepts.name: process
concepts.definition: OS abstraction: an instance of a running program with its own virtual address space, file descriptors, signal handlers, credentials.
concepts.why: Isolation unit. Processes can't directly read each other's memory (without explicit sharing). Crash containment: one process dies, others continue. The OS's fundamental abstraction.

concepts.name: thread
concepts.definition: Execution context within a process. Shares address space + file descriptors with sibling threads; has its own stack + registers + signal mask.
concepts.why: Lightweight parallelism. Thread creation/switching is cheaper than process. Shared memory is direct (no IPC needed). Cost: synchronisation responsibility moves to the programmer.

concepts.name: kernel_space
concepts.definition: Memory + privileges accessible only to the kernel. CPU runs in 'kernel mode' (ring 0 on x86). Direct hardware access; trusted code path.
concepts.why: Privileged operations (interrupt handling, memory allocation, device control) must be protected from user code. Kernel mode is the OS's enforcement boundary.

concepts.name: user_space
concepts.definition: Memory + privileges of normal application code. CPU runs in 'user mode' (ring 3 on x86). Cannot access hardware directly; goes through kernel via syscalls.
concepts.why: Isolation: application bugs can't corrupt kernel state or hardware. Memory protection enforced by MMU. The vast majority of code runs here.

concepts.name: system_call
concepts.definition: Mechanism by which user space requests kernel services: file I/O, memory allocation, process creation, networking. Linux: ~400 syscalls.
concepts.why: The user-kernel boundary. Syscall transitions are expensive (~hundreds of ns) — context switch + privilege level change. Performance-critical code minimises them.

concepts.name: context_switch
concepts.definition: Saving the current process/thread's CPU state (registers, PC, stack pointer) + loading another's. The OS scheduler's basic operation.
concepts.why: Each switch costs microseconds: CPU state save/restore + cache pollution + TLB flush (if address space changes). Frequent switching kills throughput; coarse-grained scheduling preserves cache state.

concepts.name: interrupt
concepts.definition: Hardware-triggered signal to the CPU requesting attention. Source: timer, NIC, disk, keyboard, etc. CPU saves state + jumps to handler.
concepts.why: Asynchronous I/O notification. Without interrupts, CPU would poll devices (waste cycles) or miss events. Interrupt latency is critical for real-time + networking.

concepts.name: exception
concepts.definition: CPU-triggered signal: page fault, division by zero, illegal instruction. Synchronous with the instruction that caused it.
concepts.why: Recoverable errors (page fault → kernel pages in the data) and unrecoverable (segfault → kill process). Exception handling is the kernel's response to anomalous user code.

concepts.name: PID_process_identifier
concepts.definition: Unique integer assigned to each process. Reused after process exits. Linux PIDs are 32-bit but capped (kernel.pid_max).
concepts.why: Process identification for management (kill, ps, waitpid). PID 1 is init/systemd; PID 0 is the kernel scheduler. Namespace-scoped: container PID 1 inside the namespace, real PID outside.

concepts.name: process_group
concepts.definition: Set of related processes sharing a PGID. Job control mechanism: Ctrl+C sends SIGINT to the foreground process group.
concepts.why: Terminal session management. Processes spawned by the shell join a group; the shell can signal them collectively. Critical for sane shell behaviour.

concepts.name: session
concepts.definition: Collection of process groups associated with a terminal (or none). setsid() creates new session. Daemons typically run in their own session.
concepts.why: Daemon detachment + terminal disconnection. Logging out doesn't kill the daemon because it's in its own session.

concepts.name: fork
concepts.definition: syscall creating a new process: copy of the calling process. Parent + child differ only in PID + return value of fork(). Linux uses copy-on-write for memory.
concepts.why: Process creation primitive. The 'duplicate then specialise' model: child often immediately execs into a different program. Heavyweight without COW; modern fork is fast via COW.

concepts.name: exec
concepts.definition: syscall family (execve, execvp, etc.): replace the calling process's image with a new program. Inherits PID + file descriptors.
concepts.why: fork+exec is the Unix idiom for spawning a different program. exec doesn't return on success — the new program takes over. Modern alternatives: posix_spawn, vfork.

concepts.name: wait_waitpid
concepts.definition: syscalls that block until a child process terminates. Reaps the child's exit status; deallocates the zombie entry.
concepts.why: Parent must wait or zombies accumulate. wait() gets any child; waitpid() targets specific. Modern OSes also have waitid() with finer-grained options.

concepts.name: zombie_process
concepts.definition: Process that has exited but its parent hasn't called wait. Holds only the PID + exit status — minimal resources.
concepts.why: Lets parent retrieve the exit status. Persists until reaped. Long-lived zombies indicate a buggy parent. Init (PID 1) reaps orphans inherited from dead parents.

concepts.name: daemon
concepts.definition: Background process not attached to a terminal. Typically: fork twice, setsid, redirect stdio, chdir /, close inherited fds.
concepts.why: Long-running services (sshd, postgres, nginx) need to survive logout + run independently. Standard daemonisation pattern; systemd replaces some of this with service files.

concepts.name: nice_priority
concepts.definition: Process priority hint to the scheduler. Range -20 (highest) to +19 (lowest). Default 0. Only root can decrease nice (raise priority).
concepts.why: Tells the scheduler what to favour. CPU-bound background tasks at nice 19; interactive at 0; latency-sensitive at -5 (with care). Linux's CFS interprets nice as proportional weight.

concepts.name: POSIX_threads
concepts.definition: Standard threading API. pthread_create, pthread_join, pthread_mutex_t, etc. Implemented in Linux via NPTL.
concepts.why: Cross-platform threading API. Each POSIX thread maps to a kernel thread on Linux (1:1 model). Lower-level than language threading runtimes (Go goroutines, async/await).

concepts.name: kernel_thread
concepts.definition: Thread scheduled by the OS kernel. On Linux, each pthread is a kernel thread (visible in /proc, schedulable independently).
concepts.why: The OS sees + schedules each kernel thread. Blocking syscall blocks only that thread; siblings continue. Context switch cost is significant (~µs).

concepts.name: user_thread
concepts.definition: Thread managed in user space, not visible to the kernel. Multiple user threads multiplex onto one kernel thread.
concepts.why: Much cheaper than kernel thread: switching is just register save/restore in user space. Cost: blocking syscall blocks all user threads on that kernel thread. Modern: Go goroutines, async runtimes.

concepts.name: M_N_threading
concepts.definition: M user threads mapped onto N kernel threads (M >> N). Combines cheap user-space scheduling with kernel parallelism.
concepts.why: Go's runtime, Erlang's BEAM, Java virtual threads (Project Loom). Lets programs have millions of logical threads on hardware with dozens of cores. The scheduling logic lives in the runtime.

concepts.name: thread_local_storage
concepts.definition: TLS: per-thread global variables. Each thread sees a separate copy. Linux: __thread keyword + GS register on x86_64.
concepts.why: Per-thread caches (jemalloc's thread caches, errno) without explicit lookup. Faster than locking shared globals. The GS-register-based implementation is essentially free.

concepts.name: thread_pool
concepts.definition: Fixed (or bounded) set of pre-created worker threads + a task queue. Tasks are dispatched to idle workers.
concepts.why: Amortises thread creation cost. Bounds concurrent execution. Standard pattern: HTTP servers, parallel computation, async runtimes. Tuning pool size to CPU count + workload type is key.

concepts.name: work_stealing
concepts.definition: Each worker thread has a private deque of tasks. When idle, steals from another worker's deque. Lock-free per-deque + cross-worker steal.
concepts.why: Self-balancing parallel work. Used in: Go runtime, Rust Rayon, Cilk, ForkJoinPool. Locality (private deque) + load balance (steal) — usually outperforms central queues.

concepts.name: mutex
concepts.definition: Mutual exclusion lock. lock() blocks until acquired; unlock() releases. Standard primitive for protecting shared data.
concepts.why: Easy to reason about; well-supported. Cost: contention causes blocking + context switches. Linux's pthread_mutex uses futex for fast path (no syscall when uncontended).

concepts.name: spinlock
concepts.definition: Lock that busy-waits instead of blocking. lock() loops on CAS until acquired.
concepts.why: No kernel transition; fastest when critical section is short + lock rarely held. Used in kernel + low-level code. Wastes CPU when critical section is long; backoff helps.

concepts.name: reader_writer_lock
concepts.definition: RW lock: multiple readers OR one writer. Better concurrency than mutex when reads dominate.
concepts.why: Read-heavy workloads (route tables, config caches) benefit from concurrent readers. Writers exclude all readers + other writers. More complex; can suffer writer starvation.

concepts.name: semaphore
concepts.definition: Counter with atomic decrement (wait) + increment (post). Blocks when count is 0. Generalises mutex (binary semaphore).
concepts.why: Resource counting: 'at most N concurrent users of this resource'. Producer-consumer queues. POSIX sem_t + Linux's futex-backed implementation.

concepts.name: condition_variable
concepts.definition: Signalling primitive: threads wait on a condition; another thread signals when condition becomes true. Used with a mutex.
concepts.why: Implements 'wait for state to become X'. Producer-consumer, work queues. Always loop on the condition (spurious wakeups). pthread_cond_wait atomically releases mutex + waits.

concepts.name: barrier
concepts.definition: Synchronisation point: N threads call wait(); all block until all N have arrived; all proceed together.
concepts.why: Parallel computation phases: compute → exchange → compute. Each phase ends at a barrier. pthread_barrier_t; also common in MPI for cross-process synchronisation.

concepts.name: futex
concepts.definition: Fast Userspace muTEX. Linux primitive: atomic op in user space; kernel involvement only on contention. pthread_mutex, sem_t etc. built on futex.
concepts.why: Uncontended lock costs are user-space-only (~10 ns). Contention triggers syscall (~µs). Dramatic improvement over kernel-only locks. The reason modern Linux mutex performance is competitive.

concepts.name: atomic_operations_OS
concepts.definition: Hardware-supported indivisible operations: CAS, atomic_fetch_add, atomic_xchg. Foundation of lock-free programming.
concepts.why: Build mutex, semaphore, etc. on these primitives. Lock-free data structures avoid the cost of blocking. Performance scales better under contention; complexity scales worse.

concepts.name: lock_free
concepts.definition: Algorithm guaranteeing system-wide progress: at least one thread makes progress in any finite time. No locks; only atomic operations.
concepts.why: Avoids priority inversion + deadlock. Used in high-perf concurrent containers (lock-free queues, hash tables). Complex to design correctly; the ABA problem is a common pitfall.

concepts.name: wait_free
concepts.definition: Stronger than lock-free: every thread makes progress in bounded steps. No thread can be starved.
concepts.why: Required for real-time + safety-critical systems. Even stronger guarantee than lock-free. More expensive to achieve; many problems have no known wait-free solution.

concepts.name: ABA_problem
concepts.definition: CAS sees value A, then A again; assumes no change. But value was A → B → A in between. CAS succeeds despite actual change.
concepts.why: Classic lock-free pitfall. Solutions: versioned pointers (tag bits), hazard pointers, epoch-based reclamation. Java's AtomicStampedReference exposes the solution directly.

concepts.name: deadlock
concepts.definition: Two or more threads each waiting for a lock held by another. None can proceed.
concepts.why: Coffman's four conditions: mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, circular wait. Prevention: lock ordering, timeout, deadlock detection. The classic concurrency bug.

concepts.name: livelock
concepts.definition: Threads change state continuously but make no progress. Often from naive deadlock-avoidance (back off + retry indefinitely).
concepts.why: More subtle than deadlock — CPU is busy. Two threads alternately releasing + reacquiring locks on collision. Randomised backoff + bounded retry mitigate.

concepts.name: starvation
concepts.definition: Thread is perpetually denied required resources. Other threads keep taking what it needs.
concepts.why: Common in priority systems: low-priority threads never run. Fair locks + aging (boost priority of waiting threads) prevent. RW lock with reader-preference starves writers.

concepts.name: priority_inversion
concepts.definition: High-priority thread blocks waiting for a lock held by a low-priority thread, which is preempted by medium-priority threads.
concepts.why: Famous: Mars Pathfinder. Solutions: priority inheritance (low-priority temporarily inherits high's priority), priority ceiling. Real-time OSes require these mechanisms.

concepts.name: preemptive_scheduling
concepts.definition: Kernel can suspend a running thread at any time. Time slices + interrupt-driven scheduling. The default in modern OSes.
concepts.why: Guarantees fairness + responsiveness. Misbehaving threads can't monopolise the CPU. Cost: context switch overhead + cache pollution. Tunable: shorter slices = more responsive; longer = more efficient.

concepts.name: cooperative_scheduling
concepts.definition: Threads voluntarily yield via explicit yield() call. The scheduler only runs at yield points.
concepts.why: No preemption overhead. Used in: async runtimes (no kernel involvement), some embedded RTOSes. Risk: one non-yielding task blocks the system. Go's goroutines are cooperative + use compiler-inserted yield points.

concepts.name: CFS_completely_fair_scheduler
concepts.definition: Linux's default scheduler since 2.6.23. Each task's 'virtual runtime' tracks CPU consumption weighted by nice; scheduler picks task with lowest vruntime.
concepts.why: Fair: each task gets CPU proportional to its weight. No fixed time slices — vruntime drives the decision. Red-black tree keyed on vruntime gives O(log n) selection.

concepts.name: real_time_scheduling
concepts.definition: Linux SCHED_FIFO + SCHED_RR + SCHED_DEADLINE. Priority-based, preempts SCHED_OTHER (CFS) tasks unconditionally.
concepts.why: Latency-sensitive workloads (audio, robotics, trading). SCHED_FIFO: run-to-block; SCHED_RR: round-robin within priority; SCHED_DEADLINE: EDF-based. Misuse can starve normal processes.

concepts.name: CPU_affinity
concepts.definition: Pin a thread to specific CPU(s). sched_setaffinity, taskset. Thread won't migrate to other CPUs.
concepts.why: Cache locality: thread + its data stay together. Critical for high-perf code, NUMA-aware allocation. Cost: less load-balance flexibility. Sometimes essential, sometimes harmful.

concepts.name: load_balancing
concepts.definition: Scheduler periodically migrates tasks between CPUs to balance load. Linux: periodic + idle-pull.
concepts.why: Idle CPU while another's busy = throughput loss. Migration costs cache; load balancer respects cache topology. Sometimes overrides affinity hints for global throughput.

concepts.name: NUMA_aware_scheduling
concepts.definition: Scheduler prefers placing threads on CPUs near their memory. Avoids cross-socket access penalty.
concepts.why: Remote memory access is 2x slower than local on multi-socket systems. NUMA-aware scheduling + NUMA-aware allocation together preserve local-memory advantages. Critical for large-server workloads.

concepts.name: pipe
concepts.definition: Unidirectional byte stream. Created by pipe() syscall: returns two fds (read end, write end).
concepts.why: Simplest IPC. Used heavily in shell pipelines (ls | grep | wc). Kernel buffers ~64 KB. Blocks when buffer is full (writer) or empty (reader). One-direction limitation: needs two pipes for bidirectional.

concepts.name: named_pipe_FIFO
concepts.definition: Pipe with a file system name. mkfifo() creates. Unrelated processes can connect by opening the same path.
concepts.why: Pipe semantics + file system addressability. Less common than sockets but useful for simple unidirectional inter-process streams.

concepts.name: unix_domain_socket
concepts.definition: Socket within a single host. AF_UNIX. Bidirectional, supports SOCK_STREAM + SOCK_DGRAM + ancillary data (fd passing).
concepts.why: Fast: no network stack overhead (no checksums, no fragmentation). Supports fd passing (pass a file descriptor between processes). Used by X11, Docker, systemd's communication.

concepts.name: shared_memory
concepts.definition: Memory region mapped into multiple processes' address spaces. shmget/shmat or mmap(SHARED, fd). Read/write directly.
concepts.why: Fastest IPC: no copy. Cost: synchronisation responsibility. Used in databases (Postgres shared buffers), high-perf RPC. The mmap approach is more modern; SysV shm is legacy.

concepts.name: signal
concepts.definition: Asynchronous notification to a process. ~30 signals: SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGKILL, SIGSEGV, etc. Handler runs at the next safe point.
concepts.why: Process control + error notification. SIGKILL + SIGSTOP can't be caught (forced behavior). Handlers must be async-safe (limited set of safe syscalls). signalfd lets handlers run synchronously.

concepts.name: signal_handler
concepts.definition: Function registered to run when a specific signal arrives. Limited to async-signal-safe operations (~50 functions).
concepts.why: Async-safety constraint: handler can interrupt at any point, including locked critical sections. Calling malloc inside a handler can deadlock. Real applications use signalfd or self-pipe trick.

concepts.name: message_queue
concepts.definition: POSIX or System V API for sending message-oriented IPC between processes. Boundary-preserved (vs pipe's stream).
concepts.why: Structured IPC: senders post messages, receivers extract. Less common than sockets/shm in modern code. Used in some embedded + RTOS environments.

concepts.name: virtual_memory_area
concepts.definition: VMA: kernel structure tracking a virtual address range with consistent properties (permissions, mapping source). /proc/PID/maps lists them.
concepts.why: The kernel's view of process memory layout. Stack, heap, mapped libraries, mmap regions are each VMAs. Page faults consult VMAs to decide what to do (allocate, load from file, segfault).

concepts.name: page_cache
concepts.definition: Kernel's cache of file system blocks in memory. Reads serve from cache when present; writes update cache + later flush.
concepts.why: Filesystem performance. Read 'free' RAM is mostly page cache. Repeated reads of the same file are at memory speed. Linux's free shows 'buff/cache' as page cache.

concepts.name: swap
concepts.definition: Disk space used to back virtual memory that exceeds RAM. Inactive pages written to swap; freed RAM goes to active processes.
concepts.why: Lets virtual memory exceed physical. Performance: swap is much slower than RAM. Modern advice: enable a small swap (kernel still benefits) but not as a primary capacity expander.

concepts.name: OOM_killer
concepts.definition: Out-Of-Memory killer: when memory pressure becomes critical, kernel kills processes (by 'badness' score) to free RAM.
concepts.why: Last-resort survival mechanism. Choosing which to kill: oom_score (RSS-based + adjusted). systemd-oomd, earlyoom give finer-grained pre-OOM intervention.

concepts.name: VFS_virtual_filesystem
concepts.definition: Kernel's abstraction layer over different filesystems (ext4, XFS, btrfs, NFS, ...). open/read/write/close work uniformly.
concepts.why: User code doesn't know which FS backs each file. VFS dispatches to the specific FS driver based on mount point. Same API across local + network + special (procfs) filesystems.

concepts.name: inode
concepts.definition: Index node: per-file metadata (size, permissions, owner, timestamps, block pointers). Identified by inode number within a filesystem.
concepts.why: File ≠ filename. Multiple hard links share an inode. inode is the file's identity; filename is just a directory entry pointing at it.

concepts.name: dentry
concepts.definition: Directory entry: maps a name to an inode within a directory. Kernel's dcache speeds up path lookups.
concepts.why: Path resolution: each component is a dentry. Cached aggressively (frequently-accessed paths stay in memory). Cache invalidation on file changes; subtle bugs around stale dentries.

concepts.name: file_descriptor
concepts.definition: Per-process integer index into the kernel's file table. fd 0/1/2 are stdin/stdout/stderr. Returned by open(), socket(), etc.
concepts.why: Uniform handle for files, sockets, pipes, devices. Operations (read, write, close) work the same regardless of underlying type. Per-process limit (ulimit -n).

concepts.name: mount
concepts.definition: Attach a filesystem at a directory. mount /dev/sda1 /mnt — now accessing /mnt traverses into the FS on sda1.
concepts.why: Unified directory tree across many devices/filesystems. Bind mounts (mount --bind src dst) expose one directory at multiple points. Namespaces let each container have its own mount tree.

concepts.name: block_device
concepts.definition: Storage device addressed in blocks (typically 512 B or 4 KB). HDD, SSD, RAM disk. /dev/sda etc.
concepts.why: Most filesystems live on block devices. The I/O scheduler manages requests; modern NVMe uses multiple queues (mq-deadline, kyber, none).

concepts.name: journaling_filesystem
concepts.definition: FS that logs (journals) changes before applying them. On crash, replay journal to restore consistency. ext4, XFS, NTFS.
concepts.why: Crash safety: no fsck of the entire FS after crash. Journal is small + writes are sequential (fast). Metadata journaling (default) vs full data journaling (slower, safer).

concepts.name: copy_on_write_filesystem
concepts.definition: FS where modifications go to new blocks; old blocks remain until released. btrfs, ZFS, APFS, OpenZFS.
concepts.why: Cheap snapshots (just retain old block pointers). Crash safety (old state intact until commit). Cost: write amplification (rewriting blocks rather than updating in place). Common for backup-heavy + snapshot-heavy use.

concepts.name: linux_namespace
concepts.definition: Kernel mechanism isolating one or more global resources from other processes. Types: mnt, pid, net, user, uts, ipc, cgroup, time.
concepts.why: Foundation of containers. Each namespace gives the contained processes an isolated view: own PIDs (PID 1 inside), own mount tree, own network stack, etc. Lightweight: no VM overhead.

concepts.name: cgroups
concepts.definition: Control groups: limit + account + isolate resource use (CPU, memory, I/O, network) for groups of processes. cgroup v1 (legacy) and v2.
concepts.why: Resource limits + accounting. Docker uses cgroups to cap container CPU + memory. systemd uses cgroups for service tracking. The 'how much' to namespaces' 'isolated view'.

concepts.name: container
concepts.definition: Process or set of processes running in isolated namespaces with cgroup-enforced resource limits.
concepts.why: Lightweight isolation. Shares host kernel (vs VM). Per-process overhead negligible (~milliseconds startup). Used everywhere: Docker, Kubernetes pods, systemd-nspawn, LXC.

concepts.name: docker
concepts.definition: Container runtime + image format + tooling. dockerfile builds layered images; container = mounted overlay + namespaces + cgroups.
concepts.why: Standardised container deployment. Image layers reuse common base; container startup is mounting + spawning. Replaced by containerd + cri-o in Kubernetes for production, but Docker dominates developer tooling.

concepts.name: kubernetes
concepts.definition: Container orchestrator: declarative API for deploying + scaling container workloads. Pods (process groups), Services (load balancing), Deployments (replication).
concepts.why: The control plane for container infrastructure. Scheduling, scaling, health checks, networking, secrets all declared as YAML; the controller reconciles. Standard for cloud-native workloads.

concepts.name: hypervisor_type_1
concepts.definition: Bare-metal hypervisor: runs directly on hardware. KVM (Linux kernel module), Xen, ESXi.
concepts.why: Strong isolation, near-native performance. Used in cloud (AWS Nitro, Azure Hyper-V). Each VM has its own kernel; KVM uses Linux as the host kernel + QEMU for device emulation.

concepts.name: hypervisor_type_2
concepts.definition: Hosted hypervisor: runs on top of a host OS. VirtualBox, Parallels.
concepts.why: Easier user-facing setup; lower performance than type 1. Used for desktop VM workflows. Less common in production deployments.

concepts.name: KVM_kernel_virtual_machine
concepts.definition: Linux kernel module turning the kernel into a type-1 hypervisor. Combined with QEMU (or alternatives like Firecracker, Cloud Hypervisor) for device emulation.
concepts.why: Standard Linux virtualisation. Cloud providers (AWS, GCP, OCI) all use KVM under the hood. Hardware virt support (Intel VT-x, AMD-V) makes guest execution near-native.

concepts.name: microVM_Firecracker
concepts.definition: AWS-developed minimal hypervisor based on KVM. Starts VMs in <125ms, minimal device emulation, designed for serverless workloads.
concepts.why: Lambda + Fargate underlying execution environment. Stronger isolation than containers (full guest kernel) + near-container speed. Influences the broader microVM trend (Kata Containers).

concepts.name: VirtIO
concepts.definition: Paravirtualised device interface: guest knows it's virtualised; uses optimised device drivers instead of emulating real hardware.
concepts.why: Much faster than emulating physical devices. Network, block, balloon, console all have VirtIO drivers. Standard in modern VMs (KVM, Xen, even Hyper-V Linux guest).

concepts.name: init_system
concepts.definition: PID 1 process started by the kernel. Responsible for spawning + supervising all other processes. systemd, SysV init, runit, OpenRC.
concepts.why: Boot orchestration + service supervision. systemd's parallelisation + dependency tracking + cgroup-based service tracking made it standard on most Linux distros. Controversial; technical merits drove adoption.

concepts.name: systemd
concepts.definition: Linux init system + service manager + journal logger + many other components. Heavyweight; replaces dozens of independent tools.
concepts.why: Default on most distros. Parallel boot via dependency graph. Cgroup-based service tracking gives clean accounting + signal delivery. Critics object to scope creep; proponents value uniformity.

concepts.name: proc_filesystem
concepts.definition: Virtual filesystem at /proc: per-process info (cmdline, status, fd, maps), kernel info (cpuinfo, meminfo), tunables.
concepts.why: Kernel introspection via file API. cat /proc/PID/maps shows VMAs. /proc/cpuinfo shows CPUs. Most Linux monitoring tools read here. Some entries are writable (sysctl).

concepts.name: sysfs
concepts.definition: Virtual filesystem at /sys: kernel object hierarchy — devices, bus, modules, classes. Reflects kernel data structures.
concepts.why: Device + driver attributes. /sys/block/sda/queue/scheduler shows current I/O scheduler; writing changes it. udev relies heavily on sysfs for device discovery.

concepts.name: ptrace
concepts.definition: syscall enabling one process to control another: read/write memory, registers, single-step. Foundation of debuggers + strace.
concepts.why: Debugger mechanism. gdb attaches via ptrace; strace traces syscalls via ptrace. Costs: very slow (context switches per traced event). Modern alternatives: BPF-based tracing (much cheaper).

concepts.name: seccomp
concepts.definition: syscall filtering: restrict which syscalls a process can make. Filters expressed as BPF programs.
concepts.why: Sandboxing primitive: untrusted code limited to safe syscall subset. Used by browser sandboxes (Chrome's renderer), Docker, Firecracker. Defence-in-depth.

concepts.name: linux_capabilities
concepts.definition: Decomposition of root's privileges into ~40 distinct capabilities (NET_ADMIN, SYS_PTRACE, etc.). Process can have subset of root's powers.
concepts.why: Least-privilege: grant only needed capabilities. Containers drop dangerous caps (NET_ADMIN, SYS_MODULE). Replaces 'set-root' SUID binaries with finer-grained permission.

concepts.name: VDSO_virtual_dynamic_shared_object
concepts.definition: Small library mapped into every process by the kernel. Provides fast versions of cheap syscalls (gettimeofday, clock_gettime).
concepts.why: Avoid syscall transition for common reads. gettimeofday via VDSO is ~10ns; via syscall ~300ns. Critical for high-rate timestamping (databases, tracing).

concepts.name: microkernel
concepts.definition: Minimal kernel: only essential services (scheduling, IPC). Drivers, filesystems run in user space.
concepts.why: Fault isolation: a driver crash doesn't take down the kernel. Cost: more IPC overhead. Used in: seL4, QNX (RTOS), Mach (macOS partial), GNU Hurd.

concepts.name: monolithic_kernel
concepts.definition: All OS services run in kernel space. Linux, BSD, Windows. Modules loaded dynamically but still in kernel.
concepts.why: Performance: function calls instead of IPC. Cost: bug in any kernel code can crash the whole system. Modular monolithic (Linux's LKM) is the practical compromise.

rules.name: process_isolation_via_virtual_memory
if: each process has its own virtual address space
then: processes cannot directly access each other's memory
rules.why: MMU enforces the per-process page table mapping. Different processes' virtual addresses translate to different physical frames (or none). Hardware-enforced isolation; OS can't be bypassed by buggy user code.

rules.name: thread_share_address_space
if: threads belong to the same process
then: they share the same virtual address space
rules.why: Same page table = same memory view. Lets threads communicate via shared variables directly (no IPC). Cost: synchronisation is the programmer's responsibility; data races are easy bugs.

rules.name: futex_eliminates_uncontended_syscall
if: a lock is uncontended
then: futex-based mutex acquires it without entering the kernel
rules.why: Atomic CAS in user space succeeds; no syscall needed. Only contention triggers FUTEX_WAIT (kernel). Uncontended mutex ~10ns vs kernel-only mutex ~µs. The mechanism behind fast modern locks.

rules.name: CFS_proportional_share_via_vruntime
if: task A's nice level translates to weight w_A
then: A's CPU share is proportional to w_A / sum(weights)
rules.why: CFS tracks vruntime = real time / weight. Picking lowest-vruntime gives each task proportional CPU. Mathematical fairness from a simple data structure (red-black tree on vruntime).

rules.name: M_N_threading_amortises_kernel_thread_cost
if: many user-space threads multiplex onto few kernel threads
then: thread switching cost is amortised across user-space threads
rules.why: Kernel thread switch ~µs; user-space thread switch ~50 ns. Go can support millions of goroutines on few kernel threads. Cost: blocking syscalls block the underlying kernel thread; runtime must handle this (Go's netpoller).

rules.name: deadlock_requires_all_four_Coffman_conditions
if: any of mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no-preemption, circular-wait fails
then: deadlock cannot occur
rules.why: Coffman's theorem (1971). Breaking any condition prevents deadlock: lock-free (no mutual exclusion), acquire-all-or-none (no hold-and-wait), revoke locks (preemption), lock ordering (no circular wait). Each prevention strategy targets one condition.

rules.name: priority_inheritance_prevents_priority_inversion
if: low-priority thread holds a lock high-priority thread needs
then: priority inheritance temporarily boosts low-priority thread to high's priority
rules.why: Without it, medium-priority threads preempt the low-priority thread holding the lock — high-priority is indefinitely blocked. Inheritance lets low-priority finish quickly. Mars Pathfinder's famous problem; modern RT mutexes implement this.

rules.name: namespaces_provide_isolated_view
if: a process is in its own namespace
then: it sees an isolated view of the namespaced resource
rules.why: PID namespace: container's processes see only their own (PID 1 inside). Net namespace: own network stack. Mount namespace: own filesystem tree. Foundation of containers' efficiency vs VMs.

rules.name: cgroups_enforce_resource_limits
if: a cgroup has a CPU/memory limit
then: processes in the cgroup cannot exceed the limit
rules.why: Kernel enforces at scheduling/allocation time. CPU cgroup throttles; memory cgroup denies allocation (or OOM-kills). The 'how much' to namespaces' 'isolated view'. Containers combine both for full isolation.

rules.name: containers_lighter_than_VMs
if: a workload doesn't need kernel isolation
then: containers (namespaces + cgroups) are dramatically lighter than VMs
rules.why: Container shares host kernel; VM has its own. Container startup ~10ms; VM ~seconds. Memory footprint: container ~tens of MB; VM ~hundreds. Containers won for stateless workloads.

rules.name: context_switch_dominates_short_critical_sections
if: a critical section is very short (< ~1µs)
then: spinlocks outperform mutexes
rules.why: Mutex contention triggers syscall + context switch (~µs). Short section doesn't justify the cost. Spinlock busy-waits in user space ~ns. For longer sections, the spin wastes CPU and mutex wins.

rules.name: page_cache_makes_repeated_reads_fast
if: a file is read repeatedly
then: subsequent reads hit the page cache at memory speed
rules.why: First read populates the cache from disk (slow). Subsequent reads serve from cached pages. The kernel manages cache eviction (LRU-like). Database + web server perf often dominated by cache hit ratio.

rules.name: VFS_unifies_filesystem_API
if: multiple filesystems are mounted
then: the same syscalls (open, read, write) work uniformly
rules.why: VFS dispatches based on mount point's filesystem type. ext4, NFS, procfs all expose the same API. Lets application code be filesystem-agnostic. Standard Unix design pattern.

rules.name: signal_handlers_must_be_async_safe
if: a signal handler calls non-async-safe functions
then: undefined behaviour (deadlock, corruption) can result
rules.why: Handler can interrupt at any point — including inside malloc's locks. Calling malloc from handler can deadlock. Only ~50 syscalls are async-safe (write, _exit). Modern code uses signalfd to handle signals synchronously.

rules.name: CPU_affinity_preserves_cache_locality
if: a thread is pinned to one CPU
then: its data stays in that CPU's L1/L2 cache
rules.why: Without affinity, thread migration loads cold caches at the new CPU. Affinity preserves the hot cache state. Critical for performance on cache-sensitive code; less critical for memory-bound workloads.

rules.name: OOM_killer_last_resort_only
if: memory pressure becomes critical
then: OOM killer kills processes to free RAM
rules.why: Without it, kernel allocations would fail catastrophically. OOM kills based on oom_score (size + nice + adjustments). User can pre-empt via earlyoom / systemd-oomd which kill earlier with finer policy.

rules.name: work_stealing_balances_load_with_locality
if: each worker has a private deque and steals from others when idle
then: load balances + local-work is cache-friendly
rules.why: Private deque: producer + consumer are the same thread (cache-friendly). Stealing from another worker's deque tail balances load when the steal rarely happens. Used in Go, Rust Rayon, ForkJoinPool — standard for parallel runtimes.

rules.name: VDSO_avoids_syscall_for_cheap_kernel_reads
if: a value the kernel exposes is fast to compute (e.g., time)
then: VDSO provides user-space access without syscall overhead
rules.why: gettimeofday + clock_gettime + getcpu via VDSO are ~10ns. Via syscall they're ~300ns. For high-rate timestamps (database, tracing, profiling), the difference matters substantially.

rules.name: preemptive_scheduling_guarantees_fairness
if: the scheduler is preemptive
then: no thread can monopolise the CPU
rules.why: Timer interrupt triggers scheduler at each time slice. Misbehaving thread is preempted regardless of its cooperation. Cost: context switch overhead. The bedrock of modern responsive OSes.

rules.name: shared_memory_fastest_IPC_at_synchronisation_cost
if: processes need high-bandwidth shared data
then: shared memory + synchronisation primitives beat pipes/sockets
rules.why: Shared memory: zero copy. Pipes/sockets: kernel buffer + copy. For large + frequent data exchange, shared memory wins. Cost: programmer manages synchronisation (mutex, semaphore, lock-free) vs OS-managed pipe semantics.
